expected_evidence: geological: a distinct ~12,800 cal BP sedimentary marker layer (the 'black mat') containing elevated platinum, iridium and other platinum-group-element anomalies

geological: nanodiamonds (lonsdaleite, cubic diamonds), magnetic spherules, and melt-glass/meltglass droplets consistent with high-temperature airburst formation, in Middle Eastern strata (e.g. Abu Hureyra, Syria layers)
material: disrupted or abandoned occupation horizons at Middle Eastern Epipaleolithic/Natufian sites coinciding with the YD onset, charcoal/soot layers indicating widespread biomass burning

astronomical: reconstructions/simulations of a fragmenting comet (e.g. Encke-complex debris stream) trajectory and airburst dynamics consistent with a Middle-East-region impact corridor; possible meteorite/tektite-like fallback material
genetic: megafaunal or human population bottleneck signals in ancient DNA dated to ~10,850 BC in the region
oral_tradition: later Near Eastern flood/fire/catastrophe myths speculatively linked (low confidence, model-prior) to a remembered cosmic event

iconographic: possible symbolic depictions in later Near Eastern/Anatolian art (e.g. speculative links to Göbekli Tepe pillar carvings) interpreted as commemorating the event (highly speculative, model-prior)
response.rationale: This hypothesis corresponds to the (controversial) Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis localized to a Middle Eastern site — most plausibly Abu Hureyra, Syria, which model-prior recollection (unverified) associates with published claims of meltglass, spherules, and a platinum/iridium anomaly at the YD boundary (Bunch et al. 2012; Moore et al. 2020). Using the 'younger-dryas' detectability row as the closest period match: geological (0.65) and astronomical (0.7, reflecting orbital/impact-dynamics modeling rather than direct observation) are the highest-yield evidence classes and are exactly the ones proponents of this hypothesis have cited. Material evidence (0.35) is moderate — Epipaleolithic Middle Eastern sites are sparse and taphonomically fragile at 12,800 years, but not absent (Abu Hureyra itself is a counter-example of preservation). Genetic (0.3) and oral_tradition (0.1) are weak channels: no written records exist (textual = 0.0, correctly reflecting pre-literate Middle East at this date), and any oral-tradition linkage to later myth would require millennia of transmission with no verifiable chain, so its near-absence is expected from low detectability rather than being evidence against the event. Iconographic evidence (0.1) is similarly weak and speculative. Given real published (if contested) geological/material findings exist at a matching Middle Eastern site and date, the hypothesis is falsifiable and testable evidence has plausibly survived and been found — absence of stronger corroboration (e.g., in genetic or oral-tradition channels) is well explained by intrinsically low detectability for a non-literate, ~12,850-year-old event rather than by the hypothesis being false. I suggest a blended detectability adjustment of ~0.45, weighting toward the moderate-to-high geological/astronomical channels while discounting the near-zero textual/oral channels, matching the mixed but non-trivial evidentiary record actually cited in this line of research.
